name: Millennium Park
label: Millennium Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Cloud Gate' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Cloud Gate' (way/137060274): middle (24 m across); moved 25 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/23888253: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Millennium Park' (471 m across).
notes: Downtown park with sculptures and skyline views.

text.description: Millennium Park was Chicago's top tourist destination in 2017, and it is easy to see why it works so well on a phone. Within a few minutes' walk you get a mirror-like sculpture that reflects the skyline, a curving steel walkway, fountains and tall columns, all with the Michigan Avenue buildings behind. The park opened in July 2004 and covers about 24.5 acres in the north-west corner of Grant Park. Because it sits on top of parking garages and rail lines, it is described as the world's largest rooftop garden. Expect company. Cloud Gate, the curved mirror sculpture known as the Bean, is the recommended viewpoint nearby and the park's biggest photo draw. The curved surface bends the skyline and sky into one shape, so you can take a photo that is part sculpture and part city. The north and south ends of the sculpture are the best places to frame it. For a wider view of the park, try the ledge on the west side overlooking the skating rink. If you have time, Nichols Bridgeway and Wrigley Square give two different views of the park and the buildings around it. Allow time to wait for a gap in the crowd, and take a few frames rather than one.
text.geographic_location: Millennium Park is in the Loop, Chicago's downtown, in the north-west corner of Grant Park beside Michigan Avenue. It is bounded by Michigan Avenue, Randolph Street, Columbus Drive and East Monroe Drive.
text.directions_text: The park is in the Loop, bounded by Michigan Avenue, Randolph Street, Columbus Drive and East Monroe Drive. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the Bean and its reflection. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) from the west-side ledge to fit in the rink, the sculpture and the skyline, and use telephoto (2x or more) for a tighter crop of the reflected buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (north and south ends of the sculpture; for the park skyline, the west-side ledge overlooking the skating rink). The park's most famous view: the curved mirror surface reflecting the Chicago skyline and sky, with the park and Michigan Avenue buildings around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the Bean's curve on one of the lines, so the reflected skyline sits in the upper part of the frame. Crouch slightly to keep the horizon of the reflection tidy. For a different view of the park, try Nichols Bridgeway with its curving walkway in the foreground, or Wrigley Square with the tall columns and fountain framing the buildings behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the reflection to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its detail. Wipe your lens first, and use the 0.5x lens for wide shots of the park.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late evening is best if you want fewer people in the frame. One guide says late afternoon light is best, so try more than one visit if you can.

text.access_note: The park has free admission and is a public space, but check the official site before you go for opening times and for any work or closures around the Bean and its plaza.

name: Willis Tower
label: Willis Tower
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/380868216: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Willis Tower' (153 m across).
notes: Skydeck with glass ledge boxes.

text.description:
Willis Tower, still called the Sears Tower by many Chicagoans, is a 110-storey, 1,451-foot (442.3 m) skyscraper in the Loop. It opened in 1973 as the world's tallest building and kept that title for nearly 25 years. It is still the tallest building in Chicago. Its look comes from nine square 'tubes' clustered together, with seven of them stopping short at the upper floors, so the tower steps in as it rises. The dark facade is anodized aluminium and black glass.

That stepped outline is what makes it work on a phone. Close to the base, the tall dark lines rush upwards and give a strong sense of scale. From a distance, the setbacks make a clear, recognisable silhouette. The phone icon on the map sits right on the tower's footprint, so you will be looking almost straight up at the building. Try a tall, vertical frame with the edges of the tower running towards the top corners. For a view of the whole tower, walk back to the far side of the surrounding streets (Franklin Street, Jackson Boulevard, Wacker Drive and Adams Street border the site) and shoot from there. Include a little foreground, such as a street lamp or a passer-by, to show how big it is. The Skydeck, the highest observation deck in the United States, draws more than 1.7 million visitors a year.
text.geographic_location: In the Loop, on its western edge, in Chicago. The tower fills the block bounded by Franklin Street, Jackson Boulevard, Wacker Drive and Adams Street.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from anywhere in the Loop and head for the block between Franklin Street and Wacker Drive, south of Adams Street and north of Jackson Boulevard. If you are coming from further out, head for the Loop. The tower is tall enough to be seen from a long way off, so you can steer by it. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) at the base to take in the full height. Switch to the default lens (1x) from across the street. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), save it for the stepped top section.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For a shot of the whole tower, walk back across the surrounding streets and shoot from the pavement opposite.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the tower's edges up with the vertical lines so the building does not lean too much. Hold the phone as level as you can, then tilt up slowly. Keep some sky above the top. Put something small in the foreground, such as a person or a tree, to give a sense of scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to set focus, then pull the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not turn white and the dark glass keeps its detail. Live Photos can catch passing clouds reflected in the windows.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Clear daytime gives crisp lines and bright sky. Early morning or late afternoon light can add warmth to the glass. After dusk, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a wall or post.

text.access_note: The streets around the tower are public, but the Skydeck and the building's interior may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.

name: Cloud Gate (The Bean)
label: Cloud Gate (The Bean)
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'AT&T Plaza' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/137060274: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Cloud Gate' (25 m across).
notes: Mirror-like steel sculpture in Millennium Park.

text.description:
Cloud Gate, known to nearly everyone as The Bean, is a giant polished steel sculpture by Anish Kapoor in Millennium Park, in the Loop. It was built between 2004 and 2006 and formally dedicated on 15 May 2006. It is made of 168 steel plates joined so smoothly that you can't see a seam. It measures about 10 by 20 by 13 m. Its shape is inspired by liquid mercury, and that is why it photographs so well: the surface works like a curved mirror, bending the Loop skyline and the clouds into one swirling picture. You can walk right under the arch, where a hollow in the underside, called the omphalos, multiplies and twists the reflections above you.

For the classic postcard, walk to the west side of the sculpture, on Grainger Plaza (formerly called AT&T Plaza), where the skyline sits in the curve of the steel. For a wider view of the whole Bean, step back from it within the same plaza so more of the towers behind it fit into the frame. Underneath the arch you can shoot upwards into the omphalos for a very different, abstract picture. The surface shows everything in front of it, so you will appear in your own photo. Use that on purpose, or shift a step to one side. Crowds are usually thickest from late morning, so an early start gives you cleaner reflections and fewer people walking through the frame.
text.geographic_location: Cloud Gate stands in Millennium Park, in the Loop area of central Chicago. It sits between the Chase Promenade and the McCormick Tribune Plaza & Ice Rink, a short way south of Randolph Street.
text.directions_text: There is no public transport stop right at this spot, so start from the Loop and head for Millennium Park, on the Randolph Street side. Once inside the park, the sculpture is in the open plaza between the Chase Promenade and the ice rink, and it is hard to miss. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the skyline reflection. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) under the arch or when you are close to the steel. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out a single building or a patch of reflected sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For the skyline reflection, walk to the west side of the sculpture, on Grainger Plaza (formerly AT&T Plaza), where the Bean's curved surface bends the Loop skyline, with the real buildings behind it. A step to one side changes the framing, so try a couple of spots before settling. For a wider shot of the whole Bean, step back from it within the same plaza.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the curve of the reflected skyline along one of the lines. Keep your phone low and close to your body so you take up less space in the mirror. For something different, go under the arch and aim up into the omphalos, where reflections of people and buildings are warped and repeated.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the reflected skyline to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little. This keeps the bright steel and sky from washing out. Take a few shots, because people moving through the reflection will change each frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before the crowds build up. Midday sun can cause glare on the steel, and warm days get busy from late morning.

text.access_note: Cloud Gate is in an open public park, and it is described as free and open daily. Work around the plaza may affect access, so check on the day and confirm current access on the official Millennium Park site before you go.

name: Navy Pier
label: Navy Pier
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Navy Pier' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Navy Pier' (way/24800238): edge nearest the subject (942 m across); moved 5 m off water.
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-18: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Lakefront pier with the Centennial Wheel.

text.description:
Navy Pier is a long pier reaching out into Lake Michigan from Chicago's Streeterville neighbourhood. It is 3,300 feet (1,010 m) long and covers over 50 acres of shops, restaurants, theatres, gardens and parks. It opened on 15 July 1916 as Municipal Pier and was renamed Navy Pier in 1927 to honour naval veterans of the First World War. Today it draws over nine million visitors a year, so the central areas are often busy.

For photographs, the quieter place is the far end. The far eastern tip over the lake is a further walk east. From the tip you look back towards the land with open water on several sides, and the pier's buildings and the city skyline sit behind the structure. Little blocks the horizon, and there is usually less foot traffic than in the middle of the pier. Navy Pier's own photo guide calls this a prime spot for pictures.

A good first shot is a wide view that includes the water, the length of the pier and the skyline. Then zoom in on the skyline for a tighter version. If you have time to spare, Pier Park is a second option, with its carnival rides and the Centennial Wheel (opened in May 2016, 196 feet tall) set against the skyline.
text.geographic_location: Navy Pier is in the Streeterville neighbourhood of Chicago's Near North Side, on the shore of Lake Michigan. It runs out into the lake from the lakefront.
text.directions_text: Head for Streeterville, the lakefront neighbourhood beside the pier, and make your way to the pier entrance. The far eastern tip over the lake lies about 400 m further east, so continue on foot if you want the open-water view. The pier is over a kilometre long, so allow time for the walk and expect crowds near the entrance. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the water, the pier and the skyline into one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for an everyday view of the pier's buildings. Try the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the skyline and make it look closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Navy Pier (east end, the tip of the pier over the lake). The pier's outer end looking back toward the land, with open water on several sides and the pier's buildings and the skyline visible behind the structure.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the horizon level, with the water in the lower part of the picture. Use the pier's edge or railings as a line leading into the frame. Take one wide shot for the setting and one zoomed shot of the skyline. For a different view of the pier, Pier Park shows the rides and the Centennial Wheel with the skyline behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the skyline to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks too bright. Try a panorama to sweep across the water and the buildings, and keep your arms steady as you turn. After dark, switch on night mode and rest your elbows on the railing to keep the picture sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset is a popular time, and early morning is best if you want fewer people around you.

text.access_note: The pier is a public waterfront space, but rides and events may be ticketed or have restrictions, and drones are not allowed on the pier property, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: At sunset the sun is low in the west, towards the city, so photos facing the land may be partly backlit.
The central areas of the pier are likely to be busier than the tip, especially at busy times of year.
The pier is over a kilometre long, so the walk from the entrance to the tip takes some time (follows from the 1,010 m length).

name: Field Museum
label: Field Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Museum Campus' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Museum Campus' (node/13276425737): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/24825537: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Field Museum' (276 m across).
notes: Natural history museum, home of Sue the T. rex.

text.description: The Field Museum is one of the largest natural history museums in the world, and its long white marble facade makes it an easy building to photograph. It sits on Chicago's lakefront as part of Museum Campus, alongside the Shedd Aquarium and the Adler Planetarium. That setting is the main reason it works so well in pictures. You can stand back on the lawns and fit the whole building into the frame, with trees or the reflection pool in front and the water and city skyline behind. The museum began with the artefacts shown at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition and is named after its first major benefactor, the department-store owner Marshall Field. It moved to this site in 1921 from its first home in Jackson Park. The land and building belong to the Chicago Park District. The museum's own exhibitions draw up to 2 million visitors a year, so the grounds can be busy. Take your time and look for a gap in the crowd, or shoot from a little further back where fewer people walk through. Start wide to get the full front with its columns, then move in for tighter shots of the stonework and entrance. Keep your phone level so the tall columns do not lean. Late afternoon is the best time to be there, when the light from the west falls on the building.
text.geographic_location: The Field Museum is on Chicago's lakefront, just south of downtown, in the Museum Campus park next to the Shedd Aquarium and the Adler Planetarium.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stops are listed for this spot, so head for the lakefront Museum Campus near downtown Chicago. The museum is to the north-west of it, about 4 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole facade with some lawn or water in front. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close or want more of the reflection pool. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the columns and carved detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Museum Campus (lawns and reflection-pool area in front of the museum, facing the building). The museum's marble facade with lawns, trees or fountains as foreground, and the lakefront and skyline in the background. From here you see the marble facade with grass, trees or water in front, and the lakefront and skyline behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the columns with the vertical lines so they stay straight. Put something in the foreground, such as the lawn edge, a tree or the reflection pool, and let the building fill the middle of the frame. If you want a different view, Northerly Island, a walk away across the harbour, shows the museum, Soldier Field and the skyline together with grasses and water in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the white facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the marble keeps its detail. Take a few shots in case people walk through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when the light from the west hits the facade.

text.access_note: The outdoor lawns and grounds of Museum Campus can be photographed from outside, but the museum itself is ticketed, so check the official site before you go.

name: Art Institute of Chicago
label: Art Institute
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Michigan Avenue & Adams Street' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of South Michigan Avenue and East Adams Street (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Art Institute of Chicago'.
notes: Famous museum guarded by bronze lions.

text.description:
The Art Institute of Chicago is one of the oldest and largest art museums in the United States. It was founded in 1879 and sits in Grant Park. The main building was put up for the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, and the Modern Wing by Renzo Piano, opened in 2009, later made the museum much bigger. The collection includes Seurat's A Sunday on La Grande Jatte and Hopper's Nighthawks.

For a phone photo, the classic picture is the front of the museum with its Beaux-Arts facade and grand staircase, and the two bronze lions in the foreground. The lions give you an easy foreground and make the building look properly grand. The best spot is the sidewalk across Michigan Avenue from the main entrance, where you can step back far enough to fit the lions, the steps and the entrance together, with the city around them.

This is a busy corner, so wait a moment for a gap in the people on the steps. The lions are sometimes dressed up for holidays and sports events, which can change the look of your photo. If you want something closer, go up to the lions and frame them against the main doorway and the carved detail behind. For a quieter angle than the front steps, the Nichols Bridgeway gives a view down Monroe Street with the museum and park around it. Check the current situation on the day, as things change.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in Grant Park on Michigan Avenue in downtown Chicago. The viewpoint is the sidewalk across Michigan Avenue from it, at Adams Street.
text.directions_text: No public transport stops are listed for this spot, so walk to the corner of Michigan Avenue and Adams Street from Grant Park or the downtown area of Chicago. The museum itself is about 1 minute on foot from there, to the east. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the facade, steps and both lions into one frame from across the street. The default lens (1x) gives a more natural view if the pavement is crowded. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a closer shot of the lions and the main doorway.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of South Michigan Avenue and East Adams Street (sidewalk across Michigan Avenue from the main entrance). The museum's Beaux-Arts facade and grand staircase, with the two bronze lions in the foreground. Step back towards the kerb to get the lions framing the entrance against the city.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the lions low in the frame, with the staircase and entrance behind them. Keep the building straight by lining up its vertical edges with the grid. For a different shot, walk over to the lions and photograph them close up with the main portal behind. The Nichols Bridgeway is a less crowded alternative, with a view down Monroe Street.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to set focus and exposure, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Take a few frames, as people move through the picture constantly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Lighting depends on the day and time, so check how the light falls on the facade when you arrive.

text.access_note: Indoor photography rules and access vary, so check the museum's official site before you go.

name: Shedd Aquarium
label: Shedd Aquarium
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Northerly Island Park' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Northerly Island' (relation/2914325): edge nearest the subject (1665 m across); moved 5 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/17430414: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Shedd Aquarium' (213 m across).
notes: Neoclassical aquarium on the lakefront.

text.description:
Shedd Aquarium is a classical-style building on Chicago's lakefront, and its outside is much easier to photograph than its inside. The central block is octagonal, with Doric columns across the front, a formal staircase and a dome on top. Look for the small sea-themed details in the stonework, such as dolphins, waves and shells. It opened on 30 May 1930 and became a National Historic Landmark in 1987. It sits on the Museum Campus beside the Field Museum and the Adler Planetarium.

This map's stand-here point is on Northerly Island Park, at the point beside the Adler Planetarium. From here you get an open view of the Chicago skyline across the water to the north-west, with the lakefront in the foreground. One local guide calls it the city's best free skyline view. The aquarium is just along the shore to the north-west, so it makes a natural second stop. For a frame of the building itself, walk over to the aquarium's north steps, where the columns frame the downtown skyline on one side and Lake Michigan on the other.

Inside, photography is restricted, there is no flash and the galleries are dim, so a phone does best outdoors. Check the current visitor rules before you go in.
text.geographic_location: Shedd Aquarium is on Chicago's lakefront in the Museum Campus, next to the Field Museum and the Adler Planetarium. Northerly Island Park lies just to the south, along the shore.
text.directions_text: There is no station right at this spot, so head for the Museum Campus on the lakefront and look for the Adler Planetarium. The north steps are on the aquarium itself. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the skyline and lakefront. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for a bigger sweep of water and sky, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pull the distant towers closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Northerly Island Park (the point beside the Adler Planetarium on the Northerly Island peninsula). An open view of the Chicago skyline across the water to the northwest, with the lakefront in the foreground. From here the photo shows the Chicago skyline across the water to the north-west, with the lakefront in the foreground. The aquarium is close by in that same north-west direction, but the skyline is the main subject from this point. For the building itself, use the aquarium's north steps.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the lower third line so the sky and skyline get most of the frame. Keep some shoreline or water in the foreground to give depth. For a second shot, go to the aquarium's north steps and use the columns as a frame around the skyline or the lake.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the skyline to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out. Hold the phone steady and level, and try panorama mode for the full width of the skyline.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the water. Quieter times of day also make it easier to find a clear spot on the steps.

text.access_note: The outdoor viewpoints are in public parkland and open space, but the aquarium itself may be ticketed and has photo restrictions inside, so check the official site before you go.

name: Chicago Riverwalk
label: Chicago Riverwalk
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'East Wacker Drive' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of East Wacker Drive nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/504093803: large area 'Chicago Riverwalk' (1932 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Waterfront path lined with architecture.

text.description: The Chicago Riverwalk is a public walkway along the south bank of the main branch of the Chicago River. It runs from Lake Michigan west to the Wolf Point area and Lake Street, with cafés, small parks, boat and kayak rentals and a Vietnam War memorial along the way. Building began in 2001 as part of the Wacker Drive rebuild, when the road was moved to make room for the walk. The stretch near Michigan Avenue is known as the Civic district, and it is where the Wrigley Building and Tribune Tower stand. It photographs well because the water gives you a clear gap to shoot across. The Wrigley Building's terracotta front sits with the skyline rising behind it, and tour boats add movement. Further west, the Vietnam Veterans Memorial Plaza (built in 2005) offers terraces, a waterfall and a pool, which makes a calmer subject. The newer sections from State Street to Lake Street opened in 2015 and 2016, so the walk keeps changing as you move along it. For the classic frame, stand on the river-side walkway opposite DuSable Bridge, on the side away from the Wrigley Building. Wells Street Bridge is a good second choice for a long view down the river with the skyline on both banks. Bridges are busy and the walkway can be crowded on sunny days, so allow time to wait for a clear view.
text.geographic_location: In downtown Chicago, on the south bank of the main branch of the Chicago River, just below Wacker Drive.
text.directions_text: The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the Wrigley Building and skyline across the water. Switch to 2x-5x telephoto, depending on your phone, for the terracotta details and upper floors. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) when you move to Wells Street Bridge or the memorial plaza, where you want a lot in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on East Wacker Drive (On the river-side walkway, opposite DuSable Bridge, on the side away from the Wrigley Building). The Wrigley Building's terracotta facade and the skyline rising beyond it, framed across the river. The Riverwalk itself lies to the north-west of this point.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the Wrigley Building on one third of the frame, with the towers behind and a strip of water in front. Keep the horizon level. For a different view, try Wells Street Bridge for the river corridor with the skyline on both banks and a boat or train in the shot. Vietnam Veterans Memorial Plaza is another option, with dark granite walls and steps down to the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the Wrigley Building to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour and the facade isn't washed out. At blue hour, turn on night mode and brace your elbows on the railing to keep the shot steady. A Live Photo can catch passing boats.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Blue hour, the 20-30 minutes after sunset, is recommended for glowing light and reflections near DuSable Bridge. Early morning is calmer, with lighter traffic on the bridges, according to one photographer.

text.access_note: The Riverwalk is public open space and the viewpoint is on public land, but parts may close at times, so check the official site before you go.

name: John Hancock Center
label: 360 Chicago (Hancock)
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/2250380156: the OpenStreetMap point '360 Chicago'.
notes: Skyscraper with a 94th-floor observation deck.

text.description:
The John Hancock Center, now officially 875 North Michigan Avenue but still commonly called the John Hancock Center, is a 100-storey tower on Chicago's Magnificent Mile. It stands 1,128 feet (344 metres) tall, or about 1,500 feet (457 m) to the tips of its antenna masts. It was designed by Bruce Graham and structural engineer Fazlur Rahman Khan of Skidmore, Owings and Merrill. When it topped out on 6 May 1968 it was the second-tallest building in the world, and the tallest in Chicago. Today it is the fifth-tallest in the city.

It photographs well because it is so big and so plainly built, with a dark, strong outline that stands out against the sky. The phone icon on the map is right at the building, so this is a looking-up shot. Expect to capture the lower part of the tower and the busy street around it, rather than the whole building at once. If you want the full height in one frame, walk back along the street until it fits.

The building also holds offices, restaurants and about 700 homes. Its observation deck, 360 Chicago, offers 360° views over the city and up to four states. If you go up, you can take a second set of photos from the top. Keep your phone steady against passers-by on the pavement and take a few frames, as the tower is hard to judge on a small screen.
text.geographic_location: In Chicago's Magnificent Mile district, on North Michigan Avenue, at number 875.
text.directions_text: Head for 875 North Michigan Avenue, on the Magnificent Mile stretch of the avenue. The tower is very tall, so you should be able to spot it from some distance once you are on the avenue. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit as much of the tower as you can from close up. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look, and try the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details higher up.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Point the phone upwards, keep the building in the middle of the frame, and step back along the pavement if you want more of it in view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the edges of the tower with the vertical lines so it does not lean too much. Hold the phone as upright as you can, as tilting it back makes the sides lean inwards. Include a bit of street or a passer-by at the bottom to give a sense of scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky does not turn white and the building keeps its detail. If the sky is very bright, take a second shot with the slider up to see which you prefer.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or early evening, when the light is softer and the sky is easier to expose. After dusk, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a wall or railing.

text.access_note: The building is on a public street and can be photographed from the pavement, but the observation deck is a ticketed visit, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The tower can be seen from some distance along North Michigan Avenue.
Late afternoon and early evening usually give softer light for photographing a tall building.
Tilting the phone upwards makes vertical lines lean inwards, which gridlines and holding the phone upright help to reduce.
Walking back along the pavement lets you fit more of the tower into the frame.

name: Adler Planetarium
label: Adler Planetarium
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Northerly Island' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Northerly Island' (relation/2914325): edge nearest the subject (1665 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/24825591: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Adler Planetarium' (128 m across).
notes: Best skyline view from the end of the peninsula.

text.description: The Adler Planetarium sits at the northeastern tip of Northerly Island, looking out over Lake Michigan, and it is part of Chicago's Museum Campus alongside the Shedd Aquarium and the Field Museum. It opened on 12 May 1930 as the first planetarium in the United States, and its architect, Ernest A. Grunsfeld Jr., won a gold medal from the Chicago chapter of the American Institute of Architects for the design. It became a National Historic Landmark in 1987. That history is part of why the building photographs well: it is a solid, formal shape set against open water and sky, with the downtown towers beyond. Sculptures stand around it, including Henry Moore's Man Enters the Cosmos (1980), which makes a handy foreground for a phone picture. For a quieter option with room for the skyline, walk south from the planetarium along the lakefront onto Northerly Island and turn back toward the towers. If you want a second angle, the Adler Planetarium Skyline Walk lines up the Loop towers and Willis Tower across the harbour. The wind off the lake can be strong and cold, especially in winter, so keep a firm grip on your phone and bring a warm layer.
text.geographic_location: On the northeastern tip of Northerly Island, on the Lake Michigan shore, in Chicago's Museum Campus next to the Shedd Aquarium and the Field Museum.
text.directions_text: Head for the Museum Campus on the lakefront. CTA bus 146 is an easier way to reach this stretch than driving, as parking near the Skyline Walk is reported to be difficult and costly. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the skyline and lake. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole planetarium and a big sky in one frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the towers closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Northerly Island (walk south from the planetarium along the lakefront toward the island). Open lakefront views of the downtown skyline with the sun setting behind the towers. From here you can photograph the building with the lake and sky around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the lower line so the skyline and sky fill the frame. Keep the water in the foreground for depth. For a different view, the Adler Planetarium Skyline Walk lines up the Loop towers and Willis Tower across the harbour. The planetarium's own grounds give you the building in the foreground with the towers beyond the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the skyline to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sunset sky keeps its colour. After dark, switch on night mode and rest your elbows on something solid to keep the shot steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset.

text.access_note: The Adler's outdoor area is free to walk around, but the building's opening hours vary, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: From the Northerly Island viewpoint the sun sets behind the downtown towers (taken from the viewpoint guidance).
Wind and cold off the lake can be strong, especially in winter (taken from the viewpoint notes).
Resting your elbows on something solid helps keep night-mode shots steady (general phone advice).

name: Chicago Theatre
label: Chicago Theatre
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'State Street' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of State Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/124873919: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Chicago Theatre' (86 m across).
notes: Iconic vertical marquee on State Street.

text.description:
The Chicago Theatre is one of the best-known sights in the Loop, and its tall vertical CHICAGO sign and curved marquee are easy to spot from a distance. It opened in 1921 as the flagship of the Balaban and Katz cinema chain. The architects, Rapp and Rapp, designed it in a Neo-Baroque French-revival style, and it is now the oldest surviving grand movie palace. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1979 and became a Chicago Landmark in 1983. Today it is a performing arts venue with around 3,600 seats. The marquee is often described as an unofficial emblem of the city, which is why it turns up so often in films and photographs.

For a phone photo, the classic approach is to stand on State Street, on the pavement across from the theatre. From there you can fit the whole marquee, the vertical sign and the facade into one shot, with the State Street buildings framing it on either side. If you want a different feel, try a street-level view along State Street from the corner. Some visitors also shoot from the central median, which gives a more immersive view with people and traffic around you. State Street is busy, so take care when crossing and do not linger in the road. Give yourself a few minutes to try two or three framings, because the sign is tall and the best crop depends on how many people are about.
text.geographic_location: The theatre is on North State Street in the Loop, Chicago's central business and theatre district, at 175 N State St.
text.directions_text: Make your way to North State Street in the Loop and look for the tall vertical CHICAGO sign. Cross State Street only at the proper crossings and wait for the signal. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close, since the sign is tall. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Try telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out the lettering without walking into traffic.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on State Street (sidewalk on the opposite side of N State Street from the theatre, to get the full marquee and sign). The whole marquee and the tall vertical CHICAGO sign, framed by the State Street buildings, with the theatre's facade in full view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the vertical sign up with one of them so it does not lean. Keep the marquee in the upper half of the frame and leave a little street at the bottom for scale. As an alternative, try a street-level angle looking along State Street from the corner. You could also try the central median for a centred view with people and traffic, but only if it is safe to do so.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the marquee to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the lights keep their colour and the lettering stays readable. After dark, use night mode and brace your phone against your body or a solid post to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: At night, when the marquee and vertical sign are lit up and stand out most.

text.access_note: You can photograph the outside from the public pavement; for anything inside the theatre, such as shows or visits, check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: A tall vertical sign is easier to fit in with the ultra-wide (0.5x) lens.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep bright lit signs from washing out.
State Street is busy with foot and car traffic, so crossing and standing in the median need care.

name: Tribune Tower
label: Tribune Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'DuSable Bridge' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'DuSable Bridge' (way/548266139): middle (109 m across); moved 30 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/150407241: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Tribune Tower' (116 m across).
notes: Gothic tower with embedded stones from world landmarks.

text.description:
Tribune Tower is a neo-Gothic skyscraper at 435 North Michigan Avenue, 36 floors and about 141 metres (463 feet) tall. It was finished in 1925 after a famous 1922 international design competition that drew more than 260 entries. The winning design, by John Mead Howells and Raymond Hood, has buttresses near the top and a crown-shaped finish with no spire, inspired by the 'butter tower' of Rouen Cathedral. Since 2018 the building has been converted into homes, and it is a Chicago Landmark.

It photographs well because the top is so detailed. The buttresses and crown stand out against the sky, and they are especially visible when the tower is lit at night. Low down, the stonework includes carved figures and fragments from historic sites around the world, though you will need to be close to see these. The pavement directly below is too narrow to fit the whole tower in, so the best full-height picture is taken from a distance. If you have time, the Chicago Riverwalk and the plaza by the Wrigley Building (check the exact spot on a map) give different angles that include the Wrigley Building. Keep to exterior shots, as the inside is generally not open for photography.
text.geographic_location: Tribune Tower is on North Michigan Avenue in central Chicago, just north of the river and next to the Wrigley Building. It sits within the Michigan–Wacker Historic District.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from North Michigan Avenue in central Chicago and walk to DuSable Bridge. Walk across to the north side of the river to reach the tower's front door. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the full tower from the bridge. Try telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a tight shot of the crown and buttresses. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you move close to the base or onto the Riverwalk.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on DuSable Bridge (midpoint of the bridge, looking north). A full-height view of the Gothic crown and buttresses with sky behind the tower, framed from the approach to Michigan Avenue. From here the tower rises ahead and slightly to your right, with its Gothic crown and buttresses against the sky, framed by the approach to Michigan Avenue.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and hold the phone upright, so the tower's vertical lines stay straight. Keep the whole crown in the frame with a little sky above it. Keep the phone level, because tilting it back makes the tower lean. For a different view, the Chicago Riverwalk shows the base and lower facade with the Wrigley Building and river traffic.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky stays blue instead of washed out. For the crown, zoom in with the telephoto lens rather than pinching to enlarge, which keeps the detail sharper.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Midday to afternoon usually gives even light on the facade when you face north. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on the bridge rail to keep still, so the lit buttresses show up well.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from public streets and the bridge, but the building is now residential, so check the official site before you go if you hope to see inside.
claims_not_in_sources: Looking north from DuSable Bridge, the sun is mostly behind you through the middle of the day, so the facade is usually front-lit, though nearby tall buildings may cast shadows.
Bridge railings and the footway are usually steady enough to rest your arms on for a night shot.
The view from the bridge may be busy with pedestrians and traffic, so allow time to wait for a clear frame.

name: Wrigley Building
label: Wrigley Building
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'DuSable Bridge' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'DuSable Bridge' (way/548266139): middle (109 m across); moved 30 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/17460539: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Wrigley Building' (108 m across).
notes: White terracotta clock-tower landmark on the river.

text.description: The Wrigley Building is the white, clock-topped pair of towers that stands beside the Chicago River on Michigan Avenue, and it is one of the easiest buildings in the city to photograph well. Its glazed terra-cotta facade is bright white, so it stands out against the blue sky and the darker glass towers around it. The design borrows the shape of the Giralda tower in Seville's cathedral, mixed with French Renaissance details. The two towers were built between 1920 and 1924 for the Wrigley chewing gum company. The south tower has 30 stories and stands 425 feet (130 m) tall. It carries a clock with faces pointing in all directions, each almost 6 metres across. The Tribune Tower stands directly across Michigan Avenue, so the two buildings fit into one frame. This is the classic angle, and it is right beside the building. Early morning, before about 9am, is the quietest time, and a weekday helps. At night the building is lit with floodlights, so it is worth a second visit after dark. For a different view, East Wacker Drive shows the building across the river, with the skyline behind it.
text.geographic_location: The Wrigley Building is at 400–410 North Michigan Avenue on Chicago's Near North Side, on the Magnificent Mile. It stands just north of the river, directly across Michigan Avenue from the Tribune Tower.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot. The DuSable Bridge on Michigan Avenue, where downtown meets the Magnificent Mile, is a short walk along Michigan Avenue. From there the Wrigley Building is to the north, about 2 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the facade, clock tower and river all sit in one frame. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more sky and the Tribune Tower in the same shot. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to fill the frame with the clock tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on DuSable Bridge. The white terra cotta facade and clock tower of the Wrigley Building rising above the Chicago River, with Tribune Tower alongside.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the clock tower up with a vertical line so the building doesn't lean. Include a strip of the river at the bottom of the frame. If the bridge is crowded, try East Wacker Drive for a view across the river, with the skyline behind the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the white facade to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the terra cotta keeps its detail and doesn't wash out. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on the bridge rail to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before about 9am, when there are fewer people in the frame. The building is also lit at night, which makes a good second visit.

text.access_note: The bridge and the street views are open public space; for the building's own walkways, riverside park or any interior, check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The stand-here point on DuSable Bridge is on a public road bridge with a pavement, open to pedestrians.
A steady rest on the bridge rail can help keep a phone still for night mode.
Crowds build up after mid-morning, and weekdays are quieter.

name: Marina City
label: Marina City
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'State Street Bridge' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'North State Street' (roads).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/153328601: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Marina City' (163 m across).
notes: Corn-cob shaped twin towers on the river.

text.description:
Marina City is the pair of round towers on the north bank of the Chicago River that people often compare to corncobs. Architect Bertrand Goldberg designed them, and they opened in 1963. Each tower has 65 storeys and stands 587 feet (179 m) tall. The lower 19 floors are an open spiral car ramp, and every apartment above has a semicircular balcony, so the outline is made of rounded petal shapes. That repeating curve is what makes them so easy to photograph: the pattern reads clearly even in a small phone frame. Parts of the complex became a Chicago Landmark in 2016.

The best-known angle is from State Street Bridge. From the bridge deck you look across the water to both towers rising straight out of the river, with the bridge and the river below helping to frame them. If you want an alternative, the Chicago Riverwalk gives a low, straight-on view of both towers with the river in front for depth and reflections. DuSable Bridge gives a slightly higher angle with downtown buildings around the towers. The riverwalk can get crowded in summer and during events, so pick the section directly opposite the towers. Marina City is private residential property, so photograph the outside only from public places such as the bridges and the riverwalk.
text.geographic_location: Marina City is on the north bank of the Chicago River on the Near North Side, directly across the water from the Loop. It stands beside State Street.
text.directions_text: Head for the Loop, the downtown area directly across the river from Marina City, and walk to State Street Bridge. If you are walking from elsewhere in the Loop, follow State Street north to the river. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the towers, the bridge and the river together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want both full towers and more water in one frame. Keep the towers away from the edges, where ultra-wide can stretch shapes. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to isolate the curved balconies and the rooftop crowns.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on State Street Bridge (view looking west toward the towers from the bridge deck). The two corn-cob towers rising straight out of the river, framed by the bridge and the water below.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line a tower up with a vertical line so it does not lean. Keep a little river and bridge railing in the lower part of the frame for depth. For an alternative, try the Chicago Riverwalk for a low, straight-on view with reflections, or DuSable Bridge for a slightly higher angle.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the towers to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky does not wash out and the concrete keeps its detail. At dusk, use night mode and brace your phone on the bridge railing or hold your elbows against your body to avoid blur.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or the hour before sunset usually gives softer light on the concrete and fewer people on the bridge. Around dusk you can try night mode for the lit-up rooftops.

text.access_note: Marina City is private residential property, so photograph the outside only from public spaces such as State Street Bridge and the riverwalk; if you want to go into the restaurants or venues, check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning and the hour before sunset usually give softer light and fewer people on the bridge.
The rooftops are lit at dusk, so night mode may be useful.
State Street Bridge is a public road bridge with a railing that you can brace a phone against, and the deck may vibrate slightly with passing traffic.
Ultra-wide lenses can stretch objects near the edges of the frame.

name: Jay Pritzker Pavilion
label: Pritzker Pavilion
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'BP Bridge' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'BP Bridge' (way/524270341): middle (176 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/126978545: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Jay Pritzker Pavilion' (96 m across).
notes: Gehry-designed bandshell with swirling steel ribbons.

text.description:
The Jay Pritzker Pavilion is the bandshell at the heart of Millennium Park, designed by Frank Gehry. Its ribbons of stainless steel curl outwards from the stage like a metal headdress, and above the lawn a lattice of steel trellis carries the sound system. That mix of shiny curves and criss-crossing lines gives your phone plenty to work with. The pavilion opened on 16 July 2004 and holds up to 11,000 people. It is home to the Grant Park Music Festival, a free outdoor classical series.

From this raised spot the steel shell looks like a set of sails, with the Loop skyline rising behind it. Photographers say it is also less crowded than the straight-on view from the seating area. The bridge was designed by Gehry too, partly to shut out street noise from the pavilion.

If you want a closer, more abstract picture, go down to the lawn and shoot upwards at the steelwork. A quieter alternative is the Lurie Garden, where plants can frame a partial view of the stage. Drones are not allowed over the park or pavilion.
text.geographic_location: In the Loop, in Millennium Park, on the south side of Randolph Street. Millennium Park sits in the north-west corner of the larger Grant Park, between Michigan Avenue and Lake Michigan.
text.directions_text: Head for Millennium Park on Randolph Street. The pavilion is on the south side of Randolph Street, and the BP Bridge runs along its east side. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole steel shell with the skyline behind it. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it to pick out the folds of the steel.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on BP Bridge (east side of the pavilion, looking back west toward the stage). A wider view of the pavilion's curved steel shell with the Loop skyline rising behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the stage roughly central, with the skyline filling the top of the frame. Hold the phone level so the buildings don't lean. As a different angle, try the Lurie Garden, where plants can frame a partial view of the stage across the planting.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the steel to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the shiny metal or bright sky looks washed out. Tap and hold if you want to lock focus and exposure before you reframe.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Softer light away from harsh midday sun tends to be kinder to shiny metal, so check how the steel looks on your screen and adjust the exposure if needed.

text.access_note: Millennium Park is a public park, but the pavilion and lawn can be closed to the public during some scheduled concerts and events, so check the Millennium Park schedule on the official site before you go.

name: Chicago Cultural Center
label: Chicago Cultural Cente
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/15899437: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Chicago Cultural Center' (122 m across).
notes: Landmark with Tiffany glass dome.

text.description:
The Chicago Cultural Center is a neoclassical building in the Loop that opened in 1897 as the city's main library and a Civil War memorial hall. It was turned into an arts centre in 1978. It is faced in Bedford Blue Limestone and capped by two stained-glass domes, so there is plenty to photograph both outside and in.

The highlight for most visitors is Preston Bradley Hall. Its curving white Carrara marble walls sit under a Tiffany glass dome about 12 metres across, which the Cultural Center describes as the largest Tiffany dome in the world. Elsewhere, the Washington Street entrance has a vaulted lobby with white marble and mosaics, and the Randolph Street side has a pink marble stairway with bronze balusters. The Grand Army of the Republic rotunda has its own stained-glass dome, restored in the 2021-2022 renovation.

On the outside, the west façade carries the 2017 mural "Rush More" by Kerry James Marshall, a tribute to women who shaped Chicago's culture.

For photos, look for symmetry and pattern: the domes, the marble stairs and the mosaics all reward a straight-on view. Take a few wide shots to show the scale, then move closer for details such as glass, tiles and carved stone. Keep your phone steady against a railing or your elbows tucked in when you shoot upwards.
text.geographic_location: In the Loop, Chicago's central district, on the opposite side of Michigan Avenue from Millennium Park. The building has entrances on Randolph Street to the north and Washington Street to the south.
text.directions_text: Head for the Loop and find Millennium Park, then cross Michigan Avenue to reach the Cultural Center on the west side. The Randolph Street entrance is at number 77 East and the Washington Street entrance at number 78 East. If you are coming from further away, go by taxi or hired scooter and ask for the Chicago Cultural Center. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the domes, the big marble halls and the staircases. Use the default lens (1x) for the façade and for tidy, natural-looking views of rooms. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out mosaics, bronze details and parts of the dome.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Most of your photos will be taken in and around the building itself, in the entrance halls and rooms or on the pavement outside. Interior access can vary, so check the official site before you go.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line up the centre of a dome or a staircase with the middle of the frame for a symmetrical shot. When shooting up at a dome, hold the phone level and tilt it slowly, so the edges stay straight. For the exterior, step back along the pavement and use the ultra-wide for the full façade, then zoom in on the stonework and the mural.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the glass of a dome to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the colours stay rich and the bright glass is not washed out. If the light is dim indoors, try night mode and hold very still.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Visit in daylight, when natural light comes through the stained glass. Earlier in the day is usually calmer indoors.

text.access_note: This is a city-run cultural venue with public galleries and halls, so check the official site before you go for current access to the rooms and domes.
claims_not_in_sources: Daylight shows the stained glass at its best, so a bright day is good for the domes.
Earlier in the day is usually calmer inside the building.
Photography rules and access to individual rooms may vary, so visitors should check the official site.
The ultra-wide lens helps to capture large interior rooms and staircases on a phone.

photo.artist: The original uploader was DS1953 at English Wikipedia.

name: Chicago Board of Trade Building
label: Board of Trade Bldg
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'LaSalle Street and Adams Street' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of LaSalle Street and Adams Street (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/28951633: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Chicago Board of Trade Building' (188 m across).
notes: Art Deco tower topped by Ceres statue.

text.description:
The Chicago Board of Trade Building closes the southern end of LaSalle Street, and that position is the reason it photographs so well. It is a 44-storey Art Deco tower, about 184 m (604 ft) tall, opened in 1930 and designed by Holabird & Root. The grey limestone steps back in stages as it rises to a copper pyramid roof. A three-storey aluminium statue of Ceres, the Roman goddess of grain, stands on top. It was Chicago's tallest building until 1965, and it became a Chicago Landmark in 1977 and a National Historic Landmark in 1978.

The classic picture is taken from the corner of LaSalle Street and Adams Street, looking south. The office towers on either side line up like a frame, and the tower sits in the middle at the far end. The result is a tidy, symmetrical shot that suits a phone held upright. A guide to the view also suggests going closer with a wide lens for a more dramatic angle. If you want a second option, try the corner of N LaSalle Street and W Washington Street, which gives a street-level view with the lamps lining the approach.

Stay on the pavement or a median while you shoot. Traffic on LaSalle is a real hazard, and standing in the road is not worth the picture.
text.geographic_location: In the Loop, Chicago's central business district, at 141 W Jackson Blvd. The building stands at the south end of the LaSalle Street 'canyon' of office towers.
text.directions_text: No station is given for this spot, so aim for the Loop and go by taxi or hired scooter to the corner of LaSalle Street and Adams Street. Walk down LaSalle on the pavement to reach its base at Jackson Boulevard. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full symmetrical view down the street. If the tower looks too small, use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pull it closer. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only once you are much closer, for a dramatic upward angle.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of LaSalle Street and Adams Street (corner at Adams, looking south down LaSalle). The building closing the end of the LaSalle Street canyon, framed symmetrically by the flanking office towers. From here the Board of Trade closes the end of the street, framed evenly by the office towers on both sides. Stay on the pavement or a median rather than the middle of the road.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the tower on the central vertical line so the buildings either side balance. Hold the phone level and upright so the tall sides stay straight. For a different view, try the corner of N LaSalle Street and W Washington Street, which shows the same view with the street lamps along the approach.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the tower to set focus, then use the exposure slider to stop the bright sky washing out the pale stone. If the street is in shade, lift the exposure slightly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning on a weekend, when there is less traffic and fewer parked cars.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the street at any time, but it is a working office building and the lobby is only open in business hours, so check the official site before you go if you want to see inside.

name: Crown Fountain
label: Crown Fountain
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Crown Fountain' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/3154126: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Crown Fountain' (69 m across).
notes: Video-face fountain towers in Millennium Park.

text.description:
Crown Fountain is a piece of public art in Millennium Park, in the Loop. Two glass brick towers face each other across a black granite reflecting pool. Each tower is 50 feet (15.2 m) tall and has a screen on its inward face that shows video faces of Chicago residents. The Spanish artist Jaume Plensa designed it, and it opened in July 2004. From May to October the water runs on and off, spilling down the towers and spouting from a nozzle on each front face. The fountain is also sometimes known as the "Squirting Faces".

It photographs well because there is always something moving. The faces change, the water arcs out, and children and adults play in the pool. The towers are best shot up close. Stand at the pool edge and frame one tower, with the spouting water and the pool in the foreground and the Chicago skyline behind. It is a popular subject for photographers and a common gathering place.

For your phone, wait for the face to change and for the water to start before you shoot. The screens show most clearly at the end of the day or after dark, and midday sun makes them hard to see. The water only runs in the warmer months, but the faces are on all year. Expect people in the pool in summer, and be careful with your phone near the spray.
text.geographic_location: Crown Fountain is in Millennium Park, in the Loop community area of central Chicago, at the northwest corner of Grant Park.
text.directions_text: No station or stop is listed for this spot, so start from Millennium Park in the Loop and walk to the fountain. Once you are in the park, the phone icon on the map is at the fountain itself. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for one tower with the pool and spray in front. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit both towers and the pool in one frame, or to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to isolate a single face.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand at the pool edge facing one of the two glass towers, and adjust your position by eye on site. From here you can capture a close-up of the screen face, with the spouting water and the pool in the foreground and the Chicago skyline behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the face on one of the upper lines, with the pool edge and water filling the lower part of the frame. Wait for the water to arc out before you press the shutter. Try a Live Photo to catch the face changing and the spray moving. A low phone position makes the tower look taller.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bright screen face to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the LED image does not blow out to white. After dark, night mode helps with the pool and skyline, but hold the phone steady, as moving water and people may blur.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: End of day or after dark, when the faces show most clearly. Midday sun makes the screens hard to see. The water jets only run from May to October, while the faces show all year.

text.access_note: Crown Fountain is in a public park and was designed to be highly accessible, but check the official Millennium Park site before you go for any current closures or water-feature rules.

name: Buckingham Fountain
label: Buckingham Fountain
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Columbus Drive' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Columbus Drive nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/561821879: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Clarence Buckingham Memorial Fountain' (121 m across).
notes: Grand fountain in Grant Park.

text.description: Buckingham Fountain sits in the middle of Grant Park and is one of the largest fountains in the world. It was dedicated in 1927 and built in a rococo 'wedding cake' style, inspired by the Latona Fountain at Versailles. The design stands for Lake Michigan, with four pairs of sea horses for the four states that border it. The pink marble tiers and the tall central jet make it easy to photograph, and this spot gives a calmer view than the crowded basin edge. Looking east along Columbus Drive, the fountain appears at the end of a tree-lined avenue. The trees frame it and the tower facades behind give the picture depth. If you want the full fountain in the foreground with the skyline rising behind, walk round to the fountain itself. There is also a view from the lake side that takes in Willis Tower. In season the water displays run on a regular schedule, and after dusk they are lit with colour. Outside that season the basin is empty, though it is sometimes decorated with festive lights in winter. On windy days the mist can drift well beyond the basin, so keep your phone lens dry. Take your photos from the pavement and keep well clear of the traffic.
text.geographic_location: In Grant Park, downtown Chicago, on Columbus Drive, on the stretch between the Art Institute of Chicago and Buckingham Fountain.
text.directions_text: Head for Grant Park in downtown Chicago, next to the Art Institute of Chicago. Go to Columbus Drive on the park side of the Art Institute. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the avenue, the trees and the fountain together. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pull the fountain and the buildings behind it closer together. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you move closer to the basin, as from here it makes the fountain look small.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Columbus Drive (the stretch between the fountain and the Art Institute of Chicago). The fountain seen down the tree-lined avenue, with the tower facades behind it giving a sense of depth. Stay on the pavement.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the fountain on the centre line, with a row of trees on each side. Hold the phone level so the tower facades behind don't lean. For a different view, the foreground view from beside the fountain shows the skyline behind it. Check on the day which side gives the best skyline, so try both if you have time.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the fountain to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white spray and bright sky keep their detail. Try a Live Photo to catch the jets moving. After dusk, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body for a steady shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Visit during the water-show season, roughly mid-April to mid-October, when the jets are running. Evening shows with coloured lights suit night mode. In winter the basin is empty, so expect a quieter, plainer picture.

text.access_note: The fountain stands in an open public park, but show times and the season can change, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Telephoto lenses make distant objects look closer together, so the fountain will seem nearer to the buildings behind it.
The default lens (1x) takes in the whole avenue, while the ultra-wide (0.5x) would make the fountain look small from the stand-here point.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep detail in bright spray and sky.
Evening lit shows are a good moment for night mode.

name: Chicago Water Tower
label: Chicago Water Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jane M. Byrne Plaza' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Jane M. Byrne Plaza' (way/143702452): middle (92 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/130147025: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Chicago Water Tower' (22 m across).
notes: Survivor of the 1871 Great Fire.

text.description:
The Chicago Water Tower is a small, castle-like building in pale yellowish limestone, standing right among the tall shops and towers of the Magnificent Mile. It was designed in 1869 and is about 56 metres tall. It became famous because it survived the Great Chicago Fire of 1871 while the buildings next to it burned. It is now one of the few structures from that time still standing, and it is the second-oldest water tower in the United States. Its octagonal buttresses, little crenelated turrets and parapet give it plenty of detail, and the modern glass and stone around it make a strong contrast of old and new.

The tower is the centrepiece of a small park, Jane M. Byrne Plaza. That is where most people stand to get the whole structure in the frame. Guides also point to the south side of the tower as another option, where you can fit the full height of the limestone with the Michigan Avenue buildings behind it. A further option is the street corner at Michigan Avenue and East Chicago Avenue, which shows the tower against the busy city streets. Go early in the morning if you can, as the area is quieter then. The City Gallery inside has sometimes been listed as closed, so don't plan your visit around going in. The tower is at 806 N Michigan Ave.
text.geographic_location: In the Near North Side of Chicago, on the Magnificent Mile shopping street (Michigan Avenue). The tower sits in the small park of Jane M. Byrne Plaza.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Magnificent Mile on Michigan Avenue. The tower is at 806 N Michigan Ave, and you can't miss a pale stone tower among the modern buildings. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole tower with the Magnificent Mile buildings around it. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and the top gets cut off. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the turrets and stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Jane M. Byrne Plaza (south side of the tower, plaza in front). The full limestone height of the tower with the Magnificent Mile buildings around it, framed from the plaza in front. Guides also point to the south side of the tower as another viewpoint, so you can walk round to it if you want a different angle.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the tower upright and centred, with the vertical lines on the grid, so it doesn't lean. Leave a little sky above the top. For a different view, walk to the corner of Michigan Avenue and East Chicago Avenue and shoot across the street to show the tower against the city.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the bright sky is washing out the sky and the tower's top. If you step in close with the ultra-wide, keep the phone level to limit the leaning look.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, before the area gets busy. Lit views in the evening and in winter are also recommended by one guide, though no particular standing point is named for them.

text.access_note: The tower stands in a small public park (Jane M. Byrne Plaza); the City Gallery inside has been listed as temporarily closed, so check the official site before you go if you want to go in.
